body:
People › Other ♦ Published: Yesterday; 22:39 ♦ (Vindobona)

The planned sale of Vienna-based Lukoil International GmbH (LIG) to the U.S. private equity firm Carlyle Group has fallen through. According to the 2025 annual financial statements published Tuesday in the Austrian Commercial Register, the purchase agreement signed in January 2026 expired at the end of July because the required approval from the U.S. sanctions authority, OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control) was not granted.

The sale of Lukoil International GmbH (LIG) in Vienna to the U.S. investment firm Carlyle, which was agreed upon in late January, fell through due to the lack of approval from the U.S. Department of the Treasury / Picture: © Wikimedia Commons / NVO [CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)]

For the Vienna-based holding company, whose fixed assets total over 10 billion euros according to its financial statements, the stakes are now extremely high. Should the U.S. fail to extend the existing exemptions or prohibit an alternative sale, the company faces the threat of immediate technical insolvency due to the freezing of bank accounts and cash flows.

A Game of Poker Over a Global Energy Empire

Vienna-based Lukoil International GmbH manages key international operations of its Russian parent company, Lukoil, in some 20 countries, as reported by russian news agency Interfax—including European refineries, oil fields in West Africa, and gas station networks in the U.S. and Europe. After the U.S. Department of the Treasury placed the group on the Sanctions List (SDN List) in late October 2025 as part of tightened sanctions, the group initiated emergency sales to prevent its assets from being frozen.

To enable orderly wind-downs or sales, the U.S. Department of the Treasury has repeatedly issued temporary exemption licenses (most recently General License 131J), which grant the Vienna-based holding company’s partners temporary leeway to act. The current license expires at the end of October 2026.

Trump’s Inner Circle and Kremlin Diplomacy Take Center Stage in Negotiations

While Lukoil is feverishly searching for new investors following the collapse of the Carlyle deal, investigations by leading international media outlets have highlighted the political sensitivity of the case. As the Financial Times reported, Lukoil’s international operations were the subject of direct discussions in the Kremlin. U.S. Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Vladimir Putin on September 5, 2026, to discuss not only a peaceful resolution to the war in Ukraine but also the easing of economic sanctions through the entry of new U.S. investors.

According to media reports from the Russian investigative outlet, Meduza, an investor consortium led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly (co-owner of Chelsea FC and the LA Dodgers, among other ventures) is currently considered the most promising bidder. The consortium also includes investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates with close business ties to Kushner and Witkoff. According to the media reports, the U.S. emissaries also negotiated terms under which the U.S. government could receive a direct share of the sale proceeds through an upfront payment and a subsequent profit-sharing arrangement.

Should the sale fail to receive regulatory approval before the current OFAC grace period expires at the end of October 2026, or should it be blocked again by Washington, full secondary sanctions could be imposed—a scenario that would mean the operational collapse of Lukoil’s Vienna headquarters.
